beats.intro: Alternative investments, module three. [[sub]]Private capital: funding for companies from outside the public markets, in the form of equity or debt.
beats.pe: [[a]]Private equity has three main strategies. [[lbo]]A leveraged buyout acquires a public or established private company, financing a large part of the price with debt, secured on the target's assets and serviced by its cash flows. It is a going-private transaction. In a management buyout, the current managers take part. In a management buy-in, the buyer's team replaces them. Returns depend heavily on leverage. [[vc]]Venture capital finances young companies with high growth potential. [[gc]]Growth capital, or minority equity, takes a non-controlling stake in a mature company that wants to expand or restructure. A related deal is a PIPE: a private investment in a public company. [[own]]Private equity owners have voting rights and residual claims, like public shareholders, but with more direct control over decisions.
beats.vc: [[a]]Venture capital follows the company's growth. [[pre]]Pre-seed money, often called angel investing, comes from founders, friends and family, in amounts from five thousand to five hundred thousand dollars, to develop an idea. [[seed]]Seed capital funds product development and marketing. This is where venture funds usually first invest. [[early]]Early-stage financing supports companies moving toward operation. [[later]]Later-stage financing comes after sales begin, but before an IPO. [[mezz]]Mezzanine-stage financing is the bridge to a public listing. [[pref]]Startups often raise money with convertible preferred shares. They convert into common shares later, and in a liquidation, preferred holders are repaid before common holders. Earlier stages carry more risk, so investors demand higher returns.
beats.deals: [[a]]In a buyout, the private equity firm brings capital, replaces management, installs its own board, and restructures to create efficiencies. It may buy competitors to gain scale, then exit at a much higher price. [[pipe]]A PIPE is a quick way for a public company to raise capital. In a rescue, Expedia sold one point two billion dollars of preferred shares to two private equity firms in March two thousand twenty. They pay nine point five percent, and come with warrants on eight point four million shares at seventy-two dollars. [[cost]]If Expedia redeems after two years, at one hundred two percent, and has paid no dividends, it pays about one point four five billion dollars. That is far more than a typical preferred fund yielding five point six percent. Rescue money is expensive.
beats.exits: [[a]]Private equity managers hold companies for about five years, then exit. There are two main routes. [[trade]]A trade sale to a strategic buyer. It is fast, private, and the buyer may pay a premium for synergies. But management may resist, and there are fewer buyers. [[ipo]]An initial public offering may get the highest price, keeps management on side, and lets the fund keep a stake. But costs are high, the process is long, disclosure is heavy, and a lockup can tie up capital. A direct listing skips the underwriters. [[spac]]A special purpose acquisition company is a blank-check shell that buys the company. The valuation is fixed in advance, with flexible terms and forward guidance. But dilution from warrants raises costs, and there is deal risk. [[other]]Other exits: a recapitalization, which adds leverage to pay a dividend, but is not a true exit. A secondary sale, to another private equity firm. Or a write-off, when a deal has gone badly.
beats.returns: [[a]]Private equity can offer higher returns than traditional investments. [[why]]The reasons: access to private companies, influence over management, and leverage. [[risk]]The risks are higher too: illiquidity and leverage. [[data]]But measuring performance is hard. Indexes rely on self-reporting, with survivorship and backfill biases, which tend to overstate returns. Valuations are marked infrequently, which understates volatility and correlation. Investors should look for regular, independent valuations, and require a return that compensates for the risks.
beats.debt: [[a]]Private debt is lent directly to private companies, or through a fund. Lenders receive interest and principal after a set term, and the debt is usually secured with covenants. Growth was driven by funds filling the gap left by banks after two thousand eight. Think of it as a ladder of risk. [[senior]]Direct lending sits at the top: senior, secured, with fixed payment schedules, often at a floating reference rate plus a margin. A leveraged loan is when the lender itself borrows to fund the loan. [[uni]]Unitranche debt blends senior and junior tranches into one loan, with one rate between the two. [[mezz]]Mezzanine debt is subordinated to senior debt, usually unsecured, so it pays more, and often comes with warrants or conversion rights. [[vd]]Venture debt lends to early-stage firms, as a line of credit or term loan, so founders avoid dilution. [[dist]]Distressed debt buys the debt of troubled companies, pricing in recovery. Debtor-in-possession financing funds firms already in bankruptcy, as Hertz received one point six five billion dollars at the reference rate plus seven twenty-five basis points. [[ret]]Higher returns come with an illiquidity premium, and higher risk than bonds.
beats.ltv: [[a]]Loan-to-value is key for secured private debt. A real estate fund buys six properties for one hundred million pounds, with thirty million of equity. [[loan]]A private debt fund lends seventy-five million, secured on the properties. [[ltv]]Loan to value is seventy-five over one hundred: zero point seven five. That leaves twenty-five million of excess collateral. [[chg]]As the loan amortizes, the loan-to-value ratio falls. But if property values drop, it rises, and the borrower must post more collateral to keep the ratio within the limit.
beats.vintage: [[a]]A private equity fund typically lasts ten to twelve years. [[inv]]The first five years are the investment period, when capital is called from limited partners and invested. [[harv]]The remaining years are the harvesting period, when investments are sold and capital returned. [[vy]]The vintage year is the year of the first investment. Vintage matters: funds that start in low-valuation recoveries do well, and those that deploy into booms before crashes do not. Returns by vintage ranged from about ten percent, for two thousand seven, to over forty percent for some later years. [[div]]So investors diversify across vintage years. Funds started in expansions tend to earn excess returns by funding early-stage companies, and funds started in contractions by funding distressed ones.
beats.divers: [[a]]Do private capital funds diversify a portfolio of public stocks and bonds? Somewhat. [[corr]]Their average correlations with public indexes run from point six three to point eight six. Venture capital is the lowest, around point six five. Buyouts and private debt are above point eight. [[pt]]Private capital adds a moderate diversification benefit, with a chance of excess return if you choose skilled managers. But note that part of that comes from extra leverage, market, and liquidity risk. And smoothed valuations may make correlations look lower than they are.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Private equity includes buyouts, venture capital, and growth capital, with exits by trade sale, IPO, or SPAC. [[w2]]Private debt includes direct lending, unitranche, mezzanine, venture, and distressed debt, with a premium for illiquidity. [[w3]]Both have data problems: self-reported, smoothed returns. [[w4]]Vintage year matters, so diversify across vintages. Correlation with public markets is moderate, not low.
beats.finish: Module three complete. Next: real estate and infrastructure.
